focus: 1952-05 부산정치파동의 계엄 법적 근거와 실제 지휘계통을 분리 검증

documents.provenance: US Department of State FRUS, 795.00/5-2752, telegram 1170
primary_observations: Van Fleet stated that neither he nor the ROK Army Chief of Staff had been informed or consulted in advance about the martial-law decision.
Rhee told Van Fleet that the cabinet had decided on martial law, that he approved it, and that he himself suggested including Pusan.
Rhee stated that the defense minister would issue the decree, Major General Won Yong-duk would be appointed martial-law commander, and Won would take orders directly from the President.
Rhee also stated that written orders from the Chief of Staff had not been obtained before implementation.

The telegram reports a command conflict: Chief of Staff Lee sent messages to Won and other officers countermanding the prior oral understanding and directing that the martial-law commander take no action except on Lee's instructions.

documents.provenance: National Institute of Korean History, Korean Modern Historical Materials DB, FRUS translation
primary_observations: Korean archival translation independently exposes the same telegram and confirms the non-consultation of Van Fleet and the ROK Army Chief of Staff before martial law.

documents.provenance: National Institute of Korean History Constitutional History DB
primary_observations: The 1948 Constitution Article 64 required martial law to be proclaimed pursuant to law.
Article 72(6) made declaration and lifting of martial law matters for State Council resolution.
The Martial Law Act was enacted as Law No.69 on 1949-11-24.
The legislative history says the bill was designed to require prior notification to the National Assembly for emergency martial law.

documents.provenance: Korean legal-history text / current law-history service crosscheck
primary_observations: Law No.69 was in force from 1949-11-24.
Article 1 required the President, upon proclaiming martial law, to announce the reason, type, area, and martial-law commander.
Article 21 required the President to lift martial law when the National Assembly demanded it.

documents.provenance: National Library of Korea holding guide to NARA RG84 Seoul Embassy Classified General Records 1952-63
primary_observations: The file sequence contains Law No.69, State Council Public Notice No.37 dated 1952-05-24, Proclamations No.2-6, June public-peace information, and a letter from Headquarters Martial Law Command, Yong-Nam Area, Pusan to the American Ambassador.
This establishes a concrete archival chain for recovering the domestic command documents rather than inferring them from later narratives.

documents.provenance: US Department of State FRUS, 795.00/5-3052, telegram 1200
primary_observations: The United States formally asked the ROK government to lift martial law in Pusan where EUSAK judged it militarily unnecessary.
The telegram records UNCURK's May 28 statement recommending that martial law be lifted in Pusan and detained Assemblymen be released so the Assembly could function freely.

claims.statement: The 1952 martial-law proclamation should be modeled as a multi-stage constitutional and administrative act: State Council decision -> presidential approval/proclamation -> defense-minister decree -> appointment of Won Yong-duk as martial-law commander. It is not accurately represented as a single-person act by either Rhee or Won.
insufficient_evidence: Original State Council minutes and the full original Notice No.37 scan remain unacquired.
claims.open_lead: Recover Notice No.37 and the relevant State Council minutes to identify proposal, deliberation, countersignatures, exact issue time, and territorial schedule.

claims.statement: A contemporaneous FRUS telegram records Rhee himself saying that Won Yong-duk, once appointed martial-law commander, would take orders directly from the President.
adversarial_evidence: The same telegram records Chief of Staff Lee sending messages that attempted to require Won to act only on the Chief of Staff's instructions, showing an active command dispute.
claims.attribution_boundary: This supports a claimed direct Rhee-to-Won command relationship for the martial-law regime, but does not by itself prove that Rhee personally ordered each arrest, detention, censorship action, or use of military police.

claims.statement: Van Fleet and the ROK Army Chief of Staff were not consulted in advance about the martial-law decision, and Rhee described implementation without first obtaining written Chief-of-Staff orders.
adversarial_evidence: Rhee also said he telephoned Chief of Staff Lee and obtained an oral understanding that the defense minister would issue the decree, so 'completely excluded' would overstate the record.
claims.open_lead: Recover Lee Jong-chan's messages to Won and other officers and compare their timestamps with Notice No.37 and the defense-minister decree.

claims.statement: The constitutional/legal framework clearly required State Council action and a statutory martial-law process. Secondary archival research reports a 24-hour National Assembly notice requirement and delayed documentary delivery, but the exact 1952 compliance failure should not be finalized until the operative Law No.69 articles and Notice No.37 delivery record are transcribed from primary text/image.
claims.open_lead: Extract the exact pre-notification article from the 1949 statute and the Assembly receipt/delivery record around 1952-05-25~29.

adversarial_checks: Tested whether the Army Chief of Staff had authorized the martial-law chain before implementation: FRUS says no advance consultation, but records a later oral understanding and then countermanding messages.
Tested whether Won Yong-duk's appointment alone proves personal arrest orders: no direct arrest order recovered.
Tested whether Rhee alone legally constituted martial law: constitutional-history material requires State Council action and statute-based proclamation.
Tested whether cabinet participation erases presidential agency: FRUS records Rhee's approval, suggestion to include Pusan, and asserted direct command over Won.
Tested whether US/UNC ordered the martial-law operation: Van Fleet stated he and the ROK Army Chief of Staff were not consulted; US later demanded lifting in Pusan.
Tested whether military necessity was uncontested: Van Fleet stated he saw no reason local police could not cope, and EUSAK later judged martial law unnecessary in Pusan.
Tested whether the legal-notice violation can already be marked RESOLVED: primary Notice No.37 delivery/receipt record remains missing.
Tested whether the NARA finding aid itself proves document content: it proves archival existence and sequence, not full contents.
Tested whether Chief of Staff Lee was simply part of the same command line: FRUS exposes a conflict between presidential oral arrangements and Lee's subsequent instructions.
Tested whether organization-level military-police action can be attributed to Won or Rhee individually: retained as OPEN pending orders, unit logs, and arrest records.
